elements.name: Hardware Proxy
elements.what: A class/module that encapsulates all access to a hardware device behind a device-neutral interface, hiding register layout, encoding, and access mechanics.
elements.problem: Clients scattered with direct register access break whenever the hardware changes; centralizing access in one proxy isolates hardware detail and eases porting and testing.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Hardware Adapter
elements.what: An adapter layer that converts the interface a hardware device (or its proxy) actually offers into the interface the application expects.
elements.problem: Applications written against one device interface must run with a different-but-similar device; the adapter absorbs the mismatch so neither client nor device code changes.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Debouncing
elements.what: Filtering the intermittent make/break bounce of mechanical inputs (or noisy edges generally) by accepting a state change only after it is stable for a defined interval.
elements.problem: Mechanical switches and noisy signals produce bursts of spurious transitions per actuation; naive edge handling registers many false events.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Interrupt Service Routine
elements.what: Hardware-vectored handler code that preempts normal execution to service an event, doing minimal work at interrupt context before returning.
elements.problem: Urgent, asynchronous hardware events must be handled with low latency without the CPU wasting cycles waiting for them.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Polling
elements.what: The software repeatedly samples device or data status - periodically on a timer or opportunistically in the main loop - instead of being interrupted.
elements.problem: When events are frequent, non-urgent, or interrupts are unavailable/undesirable, checking on the program's own schedule is simpler and avoids preemption hazards.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Deferred Interrupt Processing
elements.what: Split interrupt handling into a minimal ISR that acknowledges the hardware and queues work, plus deferred task-level code that completes the processing later.
elements.problem: Long ISRs increase interrupt latency and jitter for everything else; deferring the bulk of the work keeps interrupt context short while preserving responsiveness.
elements.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini & Kroah-Hartman (2005)

elements.name: Direct Memory Access (DMA) Transfer
elements.what: Configuring a DMA controller to move data between peripherals and memory without CPU involvement, with completion signaled by interrupt; often paired with double buffering so one buffer fills while the other is processed.
elements.problem: High-rate I/O consumes the CPU if every word is moved by software; offloading transfers frees cycles and meets throughput deadlines.
elements.named_in: Making Embedded Systems - Elecia White (2024)

elements.name: Cyclic Executive
elements.what: A fixed infinite loop that runs each task to completion in a predetermined order every cycle, with no preemption.
elements.problem: Small systems with stable, known task sets need utterly predictable, low-overhead scheduling without an RTOS.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Static Priority Scheduling
elements.what: Tasks receive fixed, design-time priorities and a preemptive scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready task; rate-monotonic assignment (priority by period) is the classic policy.
elements.problem: Concurrent tasks with different urgencies must meet deadlines; fixed priorities give analyzable, predictable preemption behavior.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Dynamic Priority Scheduling
elements.what: Task priorities are recomputed at runtime from urgency - classically earliest-deadline-first, where the task with the nearest deadline runs.
elements.problem: Fixed priorities cannot always achieve full utilization or handle aperiodic arrivals; deadline-driven priorities schedule optimally on one processor at the cost of predictability under overload.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Round Robin Scheduling
elements.what: The scheduler grants each ready task a turn (optionally a fixed time slice) in rotating order, giving fairness rather than urgency-driven preference.
elements.problem: When tasks have comparable importance and no hard deadlines, fair progress for all is preferable to priority starvation.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Critical Region
elements.what: Making a code region atomic by disabling interrupts or task switching (or holding a global lock) for its duration.
elements.problem: Shared data touched by ISRs or multiple tasks can be corrupted by preemption mid-update; the bluntest fix is to forbid preemption across the update.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Guarded Call
elements.what: Cross-thread service invocation performed synchronously but guarded by a mutual-exclusion semaphore so only one caller executes the service at a time.
elements.problem: Asynchronous queuing adds latency, but naked synchronous calls across threads race; serializing calls through a mutex gives timely, safe access.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Message Queuing
elements.what: Tasks communicate by posting messages into a queue that the receiver drains at its own pace, sharing information asynchronously without sharing memory access timing.
elements.problem: Direct data sharing between concurrent tasks needs locking and couples their timing; queued messages decouple producer and consumer and serialize access naturally.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Rendezvous
elements.what: An explicit synchronization object at which multiple tasks wait until a predetermined condition (e.g., all parties arrived) is met, then proceed together.
elements.problem: Independently scheduled tasks sometimes must align at known points before continuing; ad hoc flag-spinning is error-prone and unanalyzable.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Simultaneous Locking
elements.what: A task acquires all resources it will need in one atomic all-or-none step (releasing everything on partial failure), so it never holds some while waiting for others.
elements.problem: Deadlock requires hold-and-wait; grabbing the whole resource set atomically removes that condition at the cost of reduced concurrency.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Ordered Locking
elements.what: Every lockable resource gets a global order/ID and all tasks must acquire locks in strictly increasing order, making circular wait impossible.
elements.problem: Deadlock requires a cycle of waiters; imposing a total acquisition order breaks all cycles while still allowing incremental locking.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Priority Inheritance Protocol
elements.what: A task holding a lock temporarily inherits the highest priority of any task blocked on that lock, releasing the boost when it unlocks.
elements.problem: Unbounded priority inversion: a medium-priority task can preempt a low-priority lock holder indefinitely, starving the blocked high-priority task (the Mars Pathfinder failure mode).
elements.named_in: Priority Inheritance Protocols: An Approach to Real-Time Synchronization - Sha, Rajkumar & Lehoczky (1990)

elements.name: Priority Ceiling Protocol
elements.what: Each resource is assigned a ceiling priority equal to the highest priority of any task that may lock it, and locking rules built on the ceilings bound blocking to one critical section and prevent deadlock.
elements.problem: Priority inheritance alone still permits chained blocking and deadlock among nested locks; ceilings give a stronger, analyzable bound.
elements.named_in: Priority Inheritance Protocols: An Approach to Real-Time Synchronization - Sha, Rajkumar & Lehoczky (1990)

elements.name: Highest Locker Pattern
elements.what: A task locking a resource immediately runs at that resource's ceiling priority for as long as it holds the lock, regardless of who is blocked.
elements.problem: Full priority-ceiling bookkeeping is complex; raising the holder to the ceiling up front prevents priority inversion and deadlock with a simpler runtime mechanism.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Static Allocation
elements.what: All objects and buffers are allocated at compile/link time or once at startup, and the heap is never used afterwards.
elements.problem: Dynamic allocation brings fragmentation, nondeterministic timing, and out-of-memory failures that safety-critical and long-running embedded systems cannot tolerate.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Pool Allocation
elements.what: Pre-allocated pools of fixed-size blocks (often one pool per object type/size) from which objects are checked out and returned in O(1).
elements.problem: General-purpose heap allocation fragments memory and has variable timing; pools give deterministic allocation with bounded memory per type.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Fixed Sized Buffer
elements.what: Allocate memory only in one (or a few) fixed sizes - sized for the worst case - so freed blocks are always exactly reusable.
elements.problem: Variable-size heap requests interleave into unusable fragments over time; uniform block sizes eliminate external fragmentation at the cost of internal waste.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Smart Pointer
elements.what: A pointer-like object that wraps a raw pointer, validity-checks access, and manages the pointee's lifetime (typically by reference counting), releasing it when the last reference disappears.
elements.problem: Raw pointers invite dangling access, double free, and leaks; wrapping pointer mechanics in an object enforces the ownership rules mechanically.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Garbage Collection
elements.what: A runtime mechanism that finds no-longer-referenced allocations and reclaims (and, in compacting variants, relocates) them without explicit frees.
elements.problem: Manual deallocation causes leaks and dangling pointers; automated reclamation trades CPU time and determinism for memory safety. (Douglass catalogs both Garbage Collection and Garbage Compactor patterns; folded here as one mechanism with a compaction variant.)
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Finite State Machine
elements.what: Behavior modeled as a finite set of states, events, and transitions, where the reaction to an event depends on the current state.
elements.problem: Mode-dependent behavior coded as scattered flags and conditionals becomes untraceable; an explicit state model makes reachable behavior enumerable and verifiable.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation - Hopcroft & Ullman (1979)

elements.name: State Transition Table
elements.what: The state machine's transitions are encoded as a state x event table of handler/next-state entries, and a generic engine indexes the table to dispatch events.
elements.problem: Nested switch statements for large state machines are error-prone to modify; a table makes the machine data-driven, uniform in dispatch time, and auditable against the specification.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Single Event Receptor
elements.what: A state machine implementation exposing one event-receptor function that takes a parameterized event object and dispatches on current state and event type (synchronously or via a queue).
elements.problem: A uniform single entry point lets events be queued, forwarded, and processed asynchronously - the natural fit for message-driven embedded C designs.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Multiple Event Receptor
elements.what: A state machine implementation exposing one function per event type, each dispatching internally on the current state.
elements.problem: For synchronous machines, per-event functions give compile-time-checked interfaces and fast dispatch without event objects or queues.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Decomposed AND-State
elements.what: Implementing a statechart's concurrent (AND) regions by decomposing them into separate coordinated state machine objects, each handling its region's events.
elements.problem: Flattening independent concerns into one state machine multiplies states combinatorially; decomposing AND-states keeps each region's machine small and independently maintainable.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Hierarchical State Machine
elements.what: A state machine extended with nested states (behavioral inheritance of transitions from enclosing states), orthogonal regions, and history, per Harel's statechart formalism.
elements.problem: Flat FSMs explode combinatorially and repeat identical transitions in many states; hierarchy factors out common behavior and orthogonality separates concurrent aspects.
elements.named_in: Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems - David Harel (1987)

elements.name: Ultimate Hook
elements.what: A composite (super)state provides default event handling that nested substates inherit and may selectively override, mirroring how a GUI framework's default window procedure works.
elements.problem: Common policies (help, shutdown, error handling) should apply everywhere without repeating transitions in every state; the outermost state becomes the hook of last resort.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Reminder
elements.what: The state machine posts an event to itself to convert an internal condition into an explicit event that triggers further transitions.
elements.problem: Statecharts react only to events, but sometimes logically related transitions depend on conditions the machine itself computes; a self-posted reminder makes the dependency an event the topology can consume.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Deferred Event
elements.what: Events that arrive at an inconvenient state are set aside in a deferral queue and recalled for processing when the machine reaches a state that can handle them.
elements.problem: Dropping an out-of-sequence event loses information and handling it immediately corrupts the current activity; deferral preserves the event until the machine is ready.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Orthogonal Component
elements.what: Independent concurrent behaviors are implemented as separate state-machine components contained by (and exchanging events with) a container machine, instead of as orthogonal regions of one chart.
elements.problem: Full orthogonal-region support is expensive in small frameworks; composing state-machine objects gives AND-state concurrency with plain aggregation.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Transition to History
elements.what: The most recently active substate of a composite state is recorded on exit so a later transition can return to where the machine left off rather than to the default initial substate.
elements.problem: Interruptions (errors, mode changes, power cycles) should not force a workflow to restart from scratch; history transitions resume the prior context.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Run-to-Completion Event Processing
elements.what: Each event is processed fully - all transitions, entry/exit actions - before the next event is dequeued, so the machine is never observed mid-transition.
elements.problem: Allowing a new event to interrupt in-progress transition processing creates unanalyzable interleavings; RTC serializes event handling per machine and underpins queue-based event-driven designs.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)
elements.borderline: An execution-semantics rule of event-driven frameworks rather than a free-standing construct, but named, recurring, and implemented as a concrete queue/dispatch mechanism.

elements.name: One's Complement Data Storage
elements.what: Critical data is stored twice - once normally, once bit-inverted - and every read verifies the pair still complement each other before use.
elements.problem: Memory corruption (EMI, cosmic rays, stuck bits, wild pointers) silently alters safety-relevant values; a complemented copy detects corruption at each access.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Cyclic Redundancy Check
elements.what: Data blocks carry a checksum computed by polynomial division over GF(2); the receiver/reader recomputes it to detect corruption in storage or transit.
elements.problem: Large data regions and messages accumulate bit errors that simple parity misses; CRCs detect burst errors with small, cheaply computed check values.
elements.named_in: Cyclic Codes for Error Detection - Peterson & Brown (1961)

elements.name: Smart Data
elements.what: Data types that carry their own validity metadata (ranges, units, CRC) and check every set/get operation, rejecting or flagging out-of-range values.
elements.problem: Plain C data accepts any bit pattern, so faults propagate silently; building the checks into the data type enforces validity at every touch point.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Protected Single Channel
elements.what: A single end-to-end data/processing channel augmented with integrity checks at one or more points (CRCs, range checks, monitoring) so faults are detected even without redundant channels.
elements.problem: Full channel redundancy is costly; when fail-safe (not fail-operational) behavior suffices, one channel plus systematic checking detects faults at lower recurring cost.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
elements.borderline: Channel-scale structure verging on architecture, but implementable within one component and cataloged by Douglass as a design-level safety pattern.

elements.name: Dual Channel
elements.what: Two parallel channels (identical or diversely implemented) process the same inputs, with comparison or switchover logic detecting faults and continuing or safing on disagreement.
elements.problem: Single-channel systems cannot keep operating through a channel fault; replication (homogeneous for random faults, heterogeneous for systematic ones) buys fault tolerance with hardware/software cost.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
elements.borderline: Sits at the design/architecture boundary - kept per the DPESC safety-pattern canon; the system-scale redundancy variants are parked for Phase 3.

elements.name: Watchdog
elements.what: A hardware or software timer that must be periodically serviced ('kicked') by correctly running software; missing the deadline triggers reset or a safety action.
elements.problem: Hung, livelocked, or timing-broken software cannot report its own failure; an independent timer converts liveness violations into detectable, recoverable events.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Sanity Check
elements.what: A lightweight independent monitor verifies that outputs or system state remain within physically/logically plausible bounds, triggering fault handling when they do not.
elements.problem: Full result verification is often infeasible, but gross faults are cheap to catch; checking plausibility gives broad fault coverage at minimal cost.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Shared Memory Communication
elements.what: Concurrent tasks or processors exchange data through a commonly addressable memory region, coordinated by locks, flags, or hardware semaphores.
elements.problem: Message passing copies data and adds latency; for high-bandwidth or multi-processor data exchange, a shared region is the cheapest channel - at the price of explicit synchronization.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
elements.borderline: Douglass files it under distribution patterns, but as an inter-task/inter-processor mechanism it is implementable inside one program and passes the altitude test.

elements.name: Remote Procedure Call
elements.what: Invocations on a remote service are made through local stub/proxy machinery that marshals arguments, transmits, and unmarshals results so the call looks local.
elements.problem: Hand-rolled request/response messaging for every cross-node call is repetitive and error-prone; stub-generated call semantics standardize marshaling, dispatch, and error surfaces.
elements.named_in: Implementing Remote Procedure Calls - Birrell & Nelson (1984)
elements.borderline: Crosses process/system boundaries, but the stub/marshaling mechanism itself is implemented inside one component; the system topology built on it is Phase 3 territory.

parked_architecture.name: Layered Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: System-level organization of the whole software stack into abstraction layers - architecture style, POSA1/RTDP canon.

parked_architecture.name: Five-Layer Architecture Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: A specific whole-system layering template for embedded/real-time applications.

parked_architecture.name: Microkernel Architecture Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Whole-system structuring around a minimal core plus plug-in services - architecture altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Channel Architecture Pattern / Channel Pattern (RTDP ch4, DPESC ch6 base form)
parked_architecture.why: Organizes the system as sequential data-transformation channels; the base channel concept is system structure (its safety refinements Protected Single Channel and Dual Channel were kept as design elements per charter).

parked_architecture.name: Recursive Containment Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Recursive system decomposition strategy - statement about system structure.

parked_architecture.name: Hierarchical Control Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: System-wide distribution of control policy across a hierarchy of controllers.

parked_architecture.name: Virtual Machine Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Douglass presents it as an architecture pattern (portable system atop an abstract machine); the interpreter mechanism itself belongs to the GoF/language scouts.

parked_architecture.name: Component-Based Architecture / ROOM Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Whole-system component structuring per ROOM methodology - architecture altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Homogeneous Redundancy Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: System-level replication of identical channels for fault tolerance.

parked_architecture.name: Triple Modular Redundancy Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Three-channel voting redundancy - system-level safety architecture.

parked_architecture.name: Heterogeneous Redundancy Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Diversely implemented redundant channels against systematic faults - system-level safety architecture.

parked_architecture.name: Monitor-Actuator Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Paired actuation and monitoring channels - channel-pair system structure for safety.

parked_architecture.name: Safety Executive Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Centralized system-wide safety coordinator managing shutdown/recovery across subsystems.

parked_architecture.name: Broker Pattern (RTDP/POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Intermediary-based distributed system topology - POSA1 architecture canon.

parked_architecture.name: Client-Server (DPESC ch1)
parked_architecture.why: System-level role topology between requesters and providers.

excluded_notable.name: Observer / Proxy / Adapter / Mediator / State patterns as they appear in Douglass
excluded_notable.why: GoF names are canonical - cataloged once by the GoF scout; only the embedded-specific specializations (Hardware Proxy, Hardware Adapter) are entered here.

excluded_notable.name: Harmony / ROPES process (Douglass)
excluded_notable.why: Development process/methodology, not a design element - pass 7 territory.

excluded_notable.name: Rate-monotonic analysis (Liu & Layland 1973)
excluded_notable.why: Schedulability analysis technique, not an implementable mechanism; RMS priority assignment is noted as aka under Static Priority Scheduling.

excluded_notable.name: QP / QEP framework (Samek)
excluded_notable.why: A concrete framework/product realizing the patterns, not an element; belongs in the works corpus (samekcourse/samekbook already present).

excluded_notable.name: Active Object (POSA2)
excluded_notable.why: Samek's core execution model, but POSA2 is its canonical naming source - left to the POSA/concurrency scout to avoid duplicate entry.

excluded_notable.name: GoF State Pattern (DPESC ch5 'State Pattern')
excluded_notable.why: DPESC restates the GoF State pattern in C - canonical entry belongs to the GoF scout.

notes: Coverage: full ToCs of DPESC (chs 3-6) and RTDP (chs 4-9) live-verified this session (pdfcoffee/epdf ToC mirrors + O'Reilly/Pearson search confirmations); Samek's five state patterns live-verified via state-machine.com pattern PDFs and PSiCC2 search results. Yield 46 elements. DPESC chapters 3-6 fully swept: every named pattern is either an element, folded into a GoF-canonical entry (excluded_notable), or parked. RTDP: design-level concurrency/memory/resource/safety patterns in; all architecture-chapter patterns plus system-scale redundancy/distribution patterns parked (16 items) for Phase 3. Doing Hard Time's pattern content overlaps RTDP and added nothing new at title level. Charter items not found as Douglass pattern names and sourced elsewhere: DMA (Making Embedded Systems, corpus id white), deferred interrupt processing / top-bottom halves (Linux Device Drivers), priority inheritance/ceiling (Sha-Rajkumar-Lehoczky 1990), FSM (Hopcroft-Ullman), statechart/HSM (Harel 1987), CRC (Peterson-Brown 1961). Possible cross-scout duplicates to dedup at merge: message queue, smart pointer, RPC, shared memory, garbage collection, round robin, critical section. Thin spots: Samek's book beyond ch5 mostly teaches the QP framework (framework, not elements); Doing Hard Time not independently swept at ToC level; Douglass Real-Time Agility (douglassagility) not swept - likely process-heavy but could hide a few design idioms.
